JSON: Name: torture_knowledge_diffusion_pipeline Title: Comparative computational archival network analysis to identify pathways and mechanisms of transnational diffusion of modern 'white' torture techniques from French colonial counterinsurgency to later theatres Short Hypothesis: Units and jurisdictions with documented formal links to French colonial or postcolonial military training (shared personnel, instructor exchanges, or doctrinal text circulation) exhibit a higher probability of adopting specific modern torture techniques (e.g., portable electric devices, water-asphyxiation protocols, stress-position regimes, naked interrogation methods) than matched units without such links, controlling for conflict intensity and regime type. Related Work: Prior work comprises: (1) single-theatre qualitative histories documenting technique use and local practices; (2) comparative legal and human-rights reports cataloguing abuses and methods; (3) intellectual-history and discourse analyses tracing doctrines and prominent theorists; and (4) limited network- or actor-oriented studies on advisor missions and military training exchanges. Limitations in existing approaches are: heavy reliance on case-by-case, qualitative narratives that impede systematic cross-theatre comparison; sparse use of structured archival metadata or material-culture records; little integration of doctrinal/textual circulation with personnel-network evidence; absence of reproducible computational pipelines to detect technique-specific signatures across multilingual corpora and museum artifacts; and insufficient causal-testing against alternative diffusion mechanisms (e.g., parallel independent innovation, shared technological availability, or ideological affinity). Abstract: This project builds a reproducible research pipeline that integrates multilingual archival text, doctrinal publications, personnel rosters, and museum artifact metadata to quantitatively map how modern ‘‘white’’ torture techniques circulated transnationally from French colonial counterinsurgency contexts to later conflicts. The approach combines named-entity recognition and phrase-level pattern matching to detect technique mentions, embedding-based similarity and topic models to group doctrinal materials, and social-network reconstruction of instructor/advisor and officer-transfer ties. Temporal and spatial diffusion models plus regression analysis will test whether documented training or textual exposure predicts downstream adoption of specific techniques after controlling for conflict intensity and institutional factors. The primary contributions are: (1) a standardized dataset and computational methods for detecting technique diffusion across archives and artifacts; (2) network- and text-based evidence identifying the relative contribution of personnel networks versus doctrinal transmission; and (3) statistical tests of causal association between exposure pathways and adoption. Expected outcomes include reproducible mappings of diffusion pathways and quantified effect sizes for transmission mechanisms. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Digitized archival corpora in French, Spanish, English and Vietnamese comprising military manuals, course syllabi, internal reports, ministerial correspondence and published doctrinal texts (19th–21st c.); (2) personnel and training rosters listing attendees/instructors at École Supérieure de Guerre, French military missions abroad, and Argentine/Latin American staff colleges; (3) court records, human-rights reports and declassified interrogation logs that record applied techniques; (4) museum artifact metadata and images (e.g., gégène-like devices, restraints) with provenance and acquisition dates; (5) conflict-level control data (conflict intensity, regime type, troop deployments). Preprocessing: OCR + language-specific cleaning, custom multilingual NER and lexicons for technique terms, lemmatization, and manual annotation of 1,200 text samples to create gold labels. Detection pipeline: phrase-pattern matching augmented with transformer embeddings (multilingual BERT) and supervised classifier (fine-tuned) to tag technique occurrences. Network reconstruction: bipartite affiliation graphs linking personnel <-> institutions and text citation networks linking doctrinal texts by publication/translation/footnote. Analyses: (A) Descriptive: temporal curves of technique mentions per region; similarity clustering of doctrinal texts; artifact appearance timelines. (B) Causal/statistical: logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards models predicting technique adoption at unit/region-level as a function of exposure measures (personnel edge-weight, textual citation proximity, artifact imports), with controls (conflict intensity, urban vs. rural theatre, time period); include fixed effects for country and year. (C) Network inference: compute centrality metrics (betweenness, eigenvector) for nodes (institutions, instructors) and test correlation with downstream adoption rates (Spearman rho). Baselines: (1) null diffusion model (random temporal permutation of adoptions); (2) diffusion predicted only by conflict intensity and technological availability; (3) qualitative historiography-coded exposure binary. Evaluation metrics: detection precision/recall/F1 against gold labels; area under ROC for adoption prediction; hazard ratios with 95% CI; network-prediction accuracy (AUC) for node-level influence. Ablations and comparisons: (i) remove personnel-network features to evaluate textual-only transmission; (ii) remove doctrinal text features to evaluate personnel-only transmission; (iii) drop artifact metadata to test material-culture contribution; (iv) language-restricted runs (French-only vs. multilingual) to measure information loss. Validation: holdout temporal split (train on pre-1975, test on post-1975) and manual case studies cross-checked by domain historians for 30 sampled adoption events. Statistical tests: permutation tests for network correlations, likelihood-ratio tests for model comparisons, and sensitivity analyses under varying OCR-error rates. Risk Factors and Limitations: Incomplete or biased archives (missing collections, redactions, classified materials) leading to survivorship bias; OCR and multilingual NLP errors producing false positives/negatives for technique detection; ambiguous terminology across languages and euphemistic phrasing reducing measurement validity; attribution uncertainty where adoption cannot be causally linked to exposure (confounding by common third factors such as shared suppliers or concurrent international training); limited temporal precision in artifact provenance and publication dates; ethical and legal restrictions on handling, storing, and publishing sensitive material describing torture that may require access controls and IRB oversight; scalability constraints for very large corpora requiring substantial compute for transformer-based models; potential geopolitical sensitivity limiting access to key archives or to collaboration with local scholars; limited generalizability beyond the studied geographies and time windows because diffusion processes may differ in other regions or eras; risk of misinterpretation by non-specialist audiences if findings are presented without contextual historical expertise.
